1883039759.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Dense midline fibrous band formed by the decussation of aponeuroses of the anterolateral abdominal wall muscles (external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis), extending vertically from the xiphoid process to the pubic symphysis between bilateral rectus abdominis muscles.
1883039759.keyConcept: The linea alba is an avascular midline fibrous raphe separating the bilateral rectus abdominis muscles; its lack of major blood vessels makes it a preferred site for median laparotomy.

1538186718.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Triangular or slit-like opening in the aponeurosis of the external abdominal oblique muscle located immediately superior and lateral to the pubic tubercle, bounded by the medial and lateral crura and intercrural fibers.
1538186718.keyConcept: The superficial inguinal ring forms the external exit of the inguinal canal, transmitting the spermatic cord in males (or round ligament of the uterus in females) and the ilioinguinal nerve.

973304049.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Dense, curved fibrous band formed by the folded-under inferior border of the external abdominal oblique aponeurosis extending from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to the pubic tubercle.
973304049.keyConcept: The inguinal ligament (Poupart's ligament) forms the floor of the inguinal canal and demarcates the anatomical boundary between the anterior abdominal wall and the anterior compartment of the thigh (femoral triangle).

1624276668.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Cylindrical, tubular cord-like structure emerging through the superficial inguinal ring and descending into the scrotum, containing the ductus deferens, testicular and pampiniform vessels, and nerve plexuses wrapped in fascial coverings.
1624276668.keyConcept: The spermatic cord traverses the inguinal canal and acquires coverings from each abdominal wall layer: external spermatic fascia (external oblique), cremasteric muscle and fascia (internal oblique), and internal spermatic fascia (transversalis fascia).

646750718.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Prominent fibromuscular depression/pucker in the anterior abdominal wall located along the linea alba, corresponding to the obliterated embryonic site of attachment of the umbilical cord.
646750718.keyConcept: The umbilicus lies typically at the L3–L4 vertebral level, corresponds to the T10 dermatome, and represents an important portosystemic watershed area (where paraumbilical veins anastomose with superficial epigastric veins).

385557419.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Long, paired, strap-like muscle of the anterior abdominal wall running vertically adjacent to the linea alba from the pubic crest to the xiphoid process and 5th–7th costal cartilages, interrupted by transverse tendinous intersections.
385557419.keyConcept: Rectus abdominis is the primary flexor of the trunk/lumbar spine and compresses abdominal viscera; it is supplied segmentally by the lower thoracic intercostal and subcostal nerves (T7–T12).

622380622.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Tough, glistening fibrous sheath covering the anterior surface of the rectus abdominis muscle, formed by the aponeuroses of the flat abdominal wall muscles (external oblique and internal oblique anteriorly).
622380622.keyConcept: The rectus sheath encloses the rectus abdominis and pyramidalis muscles, along with the superior and inferior epigastric vessels and terminal segments of anterior cutaneous branches of intercostal nerves (T7–T12).

610846795.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Intermediate flat abdominal wall muscle visible deep to the removed external oblique, characterized by muscle fibers coursing obliquely upward and medially (superomedially) toward the costal margin and rectus sheath.
610846795.keyConcept: The internal abdominal oblique originates from the thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest, and lateral inguinal ligament; its lower fibers arch medially with transversus abdominis to form the conjoint tendon (falx inguinalis).

1899554009.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Most superficial of the three flat anterolateral abdominal wall muscles, displaying fleshy digitations arising from the external surfaces of the lower eight ribs with fibers running downward, forward, and medially (inferomedially).
1899554009.keyConcept: External abdominal oblique fibers run inferomedially ('hands in pockets' direction); its aponeurosis contributes to the anterior layer of the rectus sheath and its rolled inferior margin forms the inguinal ligament.

1698319582.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Deepest of the three flat abdominal wall muscles, identified by its horizontally (transversely) oriented muscle fibers situated deep to the internal oblique and leading into a broad medial aponeurosis.
1698319582.keyConcept: Transversus abdominis acts as a natural muscular corset, compressing abdominal contents to increase intra-abdominal pressure during forced expiration, defecation, and micturition.

1737048623.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Intermediate muscle layer of the anterolateral abdominal wall shown in cadaveric dissection deep to the reflected external oblique aponeurosis (pinned laterally), exhibiting fibers passing superomedially toward the rectus sheath.
1737048623.keyConcept: The internal oblique gives origin to cremasteric muscle loops in the spermatic cord and splits its aponeurosis into anterior and posterior laminae to encase the rectus abdominis in its upper three-quarters.

254636461.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Deepest flat muscle layer exposed through a lateral incision in the internal oblique muscle, featuring characteristic transverse (horizontal) muscle fascicles.
254636461.keyConcept: Transversus abdominis lies deep to the internal oblique; neurovascular bundles (lower intercostal nerves and vessels) run in the plane between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis.

687014281.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Prominent vertical strap muscle of the anterior abdominal wall shown in anatomical dissection both in situ within its sheath on the subject's left and as a reflected flap on the subject's right.
687014281.keyConcept: The rectus abdominis is firmly adherent to the anterior wall of the rectus sheath at its tendinous intersections, but remains free from the posterior wall, permitting passage of epigastric vessels.

614569171.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Small, paired, triangular muscle situated superficial to the inferiormost portion of the rectus abdominis within the rectus sheath, originating from the pubic crest and inserting into the inferior linea alba.
614569171.keyConcept: Pyramidalis tenses the linea alba and is innervated by the subcostal nerve (T12); it is an anatomical landmark for mid-sagittal pubic incisions and is absent in approximately 20% of the population.

762856357.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Smooth, glistening posterior fibrous wall of the rectus sheath revealed following transection and downward reflection of the rectus abdominis muscle, through which epigastric vessels course.
762856357.keyConcept: The posterior wall of the rectus sheath ends approximately one-third the distance from the umbilicus to the pubic crest at the crescentic arcuate line, below which rectus abdominis rests directly on transversalis fascia.

1427787388.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Three horizontal, transverse fibrous bands (inscriptiones tendineae) dividing the rectus abdominis into distinct segments and firmly anchoring the muscle to the anterior rectus sheath.
1427787388.keyConcept: Tendinous intersections (typically three: at xiphoid level, umbilicus, and halfway between) represent remnants of embryonic myotomic septa and adhere exclusively to the anterior lamina of the rectus sheath.

1817049846.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Midline vertical fibrous raphe seen extending in the cadaveric dissection between the bilateral rectus abdominis compartments from the xiphoid process down to the pubic symphysis.
1817049846.keyConcept: The linea alba is formed by the interlacing fibers of all three flat lateral abdominal wall aponeuroses; widening or thinning of this structure leads to diastasis recti.

678112687.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Anatomical structure indicated by its two bony attachments marked on the os coxae: the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) superolaterally and the pubic tubercle inferomedially.
678112687.keyConcept: The inguinal ligament spans between the ASIS and pubic tubercle; structures passing deep to it include the femoral nerve, femoral artery, femoral vein, and iliopsoas muscle.

1628721334.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Distinct angular indentation (incisura cardiaca) formed at the junction between the left border of the abdominal esophagus and the superior curvature (fundus) of the stomach.
1628721334.keyConcept: The cardiac notch creates the angle of His, an anatomical configuration that functions in conjunction with the lower esophageal sphincter as a mechanical barrier preventing gastroesophageal reflux.

376673837.explanation: Criteria of Identification: Long, expansive, convex lateral and inferior border of the stomach marked along its course from the cardiac notch to the pylorus.
376673837.keyConcept: The greater curvature gives attachment to the gastrosplenic ligament superiorly and the greater omentum along its inferior span; it is vascularized by the short gastric, left gastro-omental, and right gastro-omental arteries.
